title: MMP: Why Your Vote Works Weird (And How to Use It)
summary: You get two votes. One decides who runs the country. One decides who answers your angry emails. Here's why that matters.

children.text: Two Votes, Two Purposes
Under MMP — Mixed Member Proportional — you fill out two circles on election day: Party Vote: Which party should form the Government? Electorate Vote: Who should be my local MP?
The party vote is the big one. It determines how many seats each party gets in Parliament. Get 30% of the party vote, get roughly 30% of the seats (about 36 MPs).
The electorate vote chooses your local representative. There are 72 electorates — 65 general, 7 Māori. Win the most votes in your area, win the seat.
The Problem with the Old System
Before 1996, New Zealand used First Past the Post (FPP), same as the UK and US. Whoever got the most votes in each area won. Simple. Also fundamentally broken.

Three elections broke the system: 1978: Labour got more votes. National formed Government. 1981: Labour got more votes. National formed Government again. 1993: Labour got more votes. National stayed in power anyway.
Voters were tired of backing losers who won. In 1993, 54% voted to switch to MMP. The first MMP election was 1996.
How Seats Actually Get Allocated
Total MPs: 120. Electorate seats (72): Win your local area, you're in. These are decided purely by the electorate vote. List seats (48): These top up the results to match party vote proportions.

Example — 2023 Election: National got 38% of party vote → entitled to ~46 seats. They won 43 electorate seats → got 3 list MPs to reach 46. Labour got 26.9% of party vote → entitled to ~32 seats. They won 17 electorate seats → got 15 list MPs.
The Weird Stuff (And Why It Happens)
Overhang
Sometimes a party wins more electorate seats than their party vote entitles them to. They keep the extras. Parliament gets bigger temporarily.
Real example — 2020: Labour won 46 electorate seats but their party vote only justified ~43 total seats. Parliament expanded to 121 MPs until the next election.
The 5% Threshold (Or One Electorate)
To get into Parliament, a party must either: Get 5% of the party vote, OR Win at least one electorate seat.
2020: Greens got 7.9% → in. NZ First got 7.6% → in. New Conservative got 2.6% and no electorates → out, despite 62,000 votes.
Coalitions: The Price of Proportionality
Under FPP, one party often got 50%+ and ruled alone. Under MMP, that's rare. Since 1996, only one party has ever won an outright majority: Labour in 2020 (barely, with 50.01%).

How Government Formation Actually Works: Election night: We know the numbers. Negotiation phase: Biggest party talks to smaller parties. Coalition deal: Who gets what ministries, what policies happen. Confidence vote: New Government proves they have 61+ seats.

The deals: 1996-1998: National + NZ First (collapsed spectacularly). 1999-2008: Labour + Alliance/Progressive + Greens (confidence). 2008-2017: National + ACT + United Future + Māori. 2017-2020: Labour + NZ First + Greens (confidence). 2020-2023: Labour + Greens (confidence). 2023-present: National + ACT + NZ First.

Why this matters: Winston Peters held up Government formation for four weeks in 2017. He got Deputy Prime Minister and control of foreign affairs. ACT got regulatory reform and David Seymour as Associate Education Minister. Small parties leverage their seats for real power.
The Honest Assessment: Pros and Cons

What Works: Fairness — Parliament looks like the electorate (roughly). No wasted votes — 7.6% gets you 7.6% of seats, not zero. More choice — Split tickets, support small parties, still matter. Cooperation required — Parties have to work together. Diversity — More women, Māori, and minority MPs than under FPP.

What Doesn't: Complexity — Two votes confuses people (especially new voters). Kingmakers — Small parties extract concessions disproportionate to their size. Instability — Coalitions collapse (1998, almost 2005, 2017 was messy). List MPs — Not directly accountable to voters, chosen by party hierarchy. Threshold unfairness — 4.9% gets you nothing; 5.1% gets you seats.
The Bottom Line
MMP isn't perfect. The 5% threshold is arbitrary. List MPs aren't directly elected. Coalitions can be messy.
But it beats the alternative. Your vote actually matters proportionally. Small parties can win representation. Parliament looks more like New Zealand.
What to do: Party vote: The party whose vision you support nationally. Electorate vote: The person you want answering your emails locally. They can be the same. They can be different. It's up to you.

keyPoints: You get two votes: Party vote decides Parliament makeup, Electorate vote decides your local MP
A party needs 5% of party vote OR one electorate seat to enter Parliament
Coalitions are normal — small parties often hold balance of power
Since 1996, only one party has won outright majority (Labour 2020 with 50.01%)
